//: The SHARED cross-check fixture for Task 14d.
Two implementations answer the same documents over the same data: the
SQL compiler (backend/app/expressions/). Both read THIS file, and both
assert the keys in each case's `expect`.
`expect` is derived BY HAND, from the semantics written down in
evaluate.ts's docstring -- never from running either implementation.
That is the whole point: two implementations that agree with each other
and disagree with the intent prove nothing. Each case carries `why`,
Field ids name entity/relationship types by `@<name>`; each side
substitutes the ids it actually has (real bigints on the server,
synthetic ones in the browser test).
Note `u3.hired`: the string 'not-a-date' is stored in a `date`
attribute. That is NOT a hole in the fixture -- `entity_validate`
time, so the database genuinely permits it, and any compiler that casts
an attribute to `date` errors on this row.

cases.name: integer_lt_compares_as_a_number_not_as_text
cases.why: cap is integer: 9 < 10, 10 and 100 are not. A text comparison would say '100' < '10' < '9' and answer u2,u3.

cases.name: integer_lt_separates_a_numeric_order_from_a_text_one
cases.why: The caps are 9, 10 and 100. As numbers, 9 and 10 are below 100. As TEXT they would order '10' < '100' < '9', so a text comparison against '100' would answer u2 alone -- a different, non-empty answer, which is what makes this case discriminate rather than merely pass. (v1's `text` type offers no ordering operators at all -- see OPERATORS_BY_TYPE in operators.ts -- so the reverse direction, text ordering, is pinned by the `date` cases below, which are ordered AS text by design.)

cases.name: at_most_on_an_integer_attribute
cases.why: 9 and 10 are at most 10; 100 is not.

cases.name: time_equality_ignores_the_seconds_spelling
cases.why: Ruling 36. u1 stores '09:30' and u2 '09:30:00'; both ARE 09:30. A string equality would answer u1 alone.

cases.name: a_missing_key_and_a_stored_null_are_both_absent
cases.why: u1 stores note: null, u2 has no note key at all. Both are absent, so both match 'is empty'. u3 has 'hi'. The shifts have no unit.note either, but the rule is about a unit, and a rule about another type's attribute is false whatever the operator.

cases.name: is_not_empty_is_the_exact_complement_within_the_type
cases.why: Only u3 has a note. The shifts are still excluded: the rule is about unit.note.

cases.name: an_absent_value_equals_nothing
cases.why: u1's note is a stored null and u2's is missing; neither equals 'hi'. Only u3 does.

cases.name: text_equality_is_case_sensitive
cases.why: u1's label is 'Alice', u2's is 'alice'. SQL '=' on text is case sensitive.

cases.name: contains_is_case_insensitive
cases.why: 'Alice' and 'alice' both contain 'ali' when case is folded. 'Morning'/'Night' do not; u3's label is null.

cases.name: a_percent_in_contains_is_a_character_not_a_wildcard
cases.why: Only u3's code contains a literal '%'. An unescaped LIKE pattern would be '%%%', which matches every unit.

cases.name: an_underscore_in_contains_is_a_character_not_a_wildcard
cases.why: No code contains '_'. An unescaped LIKE pattern '%_%' matches every non-empty code.

cases.name: year_of_a_date
cases.why: u1 was hired in 2024, u2 in 2023, and u3's stored value is not a date at all, so it has no year.

cases.name: month_of_a_date
cases.why: Only u2's 2023-12-31 is in month 12.

cases.name: day_of_a_date
cases.why: u1 is the 5th.

cases.name: a_date_comparison_is_a_text_comparison_including_for_a_non_date
cases.why: ISO dates are zero-padded, so ordering them as text IS chronological -- which is what the client does. u1's 2024-03-05 is after 2024-01-01; u2's 2023-12-31 is not; and u3's 'not-a-date' begins with 'n', which sorts after '2'. The third row is the point: a compiler that cast this column to date would raise, not answer.

cases.name: hour_of_a_time
cases.why: u1 09:30 and u2 09:30:00 are both hour 9; u3 is 23.

cases.name: minute_of_a_time
cases.why: Only u3's 23:59 has minute 59.

cases.name: lower_of_a_column
cases.why: 'Alice' and 'alice' both lower-case to 'alice'. u3's label is null, so lower() of it is absent.

cases.name: upper_of_a_column
cases.why: Only u1's key upper-cases to 'U1'.

cases.name: length_of_a_text_attribute
cases.why: '10' is two characters; '9' is one; 'hello%world' is eleven. The shifts have a cap too, and it is text, but this rule names unit.code.

cases.name: abs_of_a_number_attribute
cases.why: 2.5 and -2.5 both have absolute value 2.5; u3's ratio is 0.

cases.name: abs_of_an_integer_column_spans_both_types
cases.why: sort_order is a column every entity has, so this rule is not narrowed to one type: u1 and s1 are both 1.

cases.name: enum_is_one_of
cases.why: u1 is a, u2 is b, u3 is c.

cases.name: enum_is_not_one_of
cases.why: u3 is the only unit whose grade is outside {a,b}. The shifts have no grade at all and the rule is a unit's, so they are excluded -- 'is not one of' is not 'has no value'.

cases.name: boolean_attribute
cases.why: u1 and u3 are live; u2 is not.

cases.name: boolean_column_spans_both_types
cases.why: Only u3 is inactive.

cases.name: count_outgoing_relationships
cases.why: u1 covers s1 and s2 (2), u2 covers s1 (1), u3 covers nothing (0). A count is never narrowed to an entity type, but no shift is the FROM end of a covers row, so the shifts are 0.

cases.name: count_incoming_relationships
cases.why: s1 is covered twice, s2 once. Exactly one incoming is s2.

cases.name: count_in_either_direction_is_zero_not_absent
cases.why: u3 is at neither end of any covers row. Zero is a count, not an absent value, so = 0 selects it rather than nothing.

cases.name: not_inverts_a_false_rule_including_for_the_wrong_type
cases.why: The inner rule is true only for u1. Everything else is false -- u2 and u3 because 10 and 100 are not < 10, the shifts because a rule about unit.cap is false for a shift -- so the negation selects all four. In SQL this is the three-valued-logic trap: an absent value makes the inner predicate NULL, and NOT NULL is NULL, which would drop rows the client keeps.

cases.name: not_over_an_absent_value
cases.why: 'note is empty' is true for u1 and u2 and false for everything else, so its negation is u3 and the two shifts.

cases.name: not_over_an_empty_group_matches_nothing
cases.why: An empty group is no constraint, i.e. true, so its negation is false for every row.

cases.name: or_across_two_entity_types
cases.why: u1's cap is 9; s2's cap is the text '10'. The two rules name different types' attributes, which is fine under or.

cases.name: and_across_two_entity_types_matches_nothing
cases.why: An entity has exactly one type, so no row can satisfy a unit rule and a shift rule at once. The client warns about this shape; it does not refuse it.

cases.name: the_same_attribute_name_on_two_types_is_two_fields
cases.why: unit.cap is an integer and shift.cap is text. This rule names the shift's, so it compares text: '9' and '10' are the two shifts, and only s1 is '9'.

cases.name: an_empty_document_constrains_nothing
cases.why: No rules means no filter, not an impossible one.

cases.name: a_nested_group
cases.why: Active entities are u1, u2, s1, s2. Of those, u1 has cap 9 and s2 starts at 22:00, which is after 20:00; s1's 06:00 is not, and u2's cap is 10.

cases.name: not_equal_on_a_column
cases.why: Every key but u1.

cases.name: at_least_on_an_integer_column
cases.why: sort_order 2 or more: u2, u3, s2.

cases.name: a_negative_number_attribute
cases.why: Only u2's ratio is below zero.

cases.name: begins_with_is_case_insensitive
cases.why: The three unit keys begin with 'u'; folding case makes 'U' match them too.

cases.name: ends_with
cases.why: u1 and s1 end in '1'.

cases.name: does_not_contain_on_a_non_null_column
cases.why: key is NOT NULL and never absent, so the complement of 'contains u' is exactly the two shifts.

cases.name: not_equal_on_a_time_uses_the_time_comparison
cases.why: u1 and u2 both ARE 09:30, however they are spelled, so only u3 differs. A string != would wrongly include u2.

cases.name: not_over_a_comparison_whose_value_is_absent
cases.why: The inner rule is true only for u3. It is FALSE for u1 (note is a stored null), for u2 (no note key) and for the two shifts (a rule about a unit), so the negation selects those four. This is the exact three-valued-logic trap: in SQL the inner predicate is NULL for u1 and u2 -- the value is absent, so the comparison has no answer -- and NOT NULL is NULL, which drops both rows. The earlier `not` cases do not reach it: their inner predicate is false rather than null, because the entity-type narrowing is false or the compared value is present.

cases.name: length_counts_spaces
cases.why: The tags are ' a ', 'ab' and 'abc'. Three characters is u1 (with its two spaces) and u3. A length that trimmed first would answer u3 alone.

cases.name: hour_of_a_time_the_database_would_read_and_the_app_would_not
cases.why: u1's ends is 09:30:00. u2's is '9:5', which Postgres WOULD accept as 09:05 and the client would not accept at all (its clock regexp wants two digits in each field), so the two would disagree unless the server checks the spelling before it casts. u3 has no ends. entity_validate permits both, since it checks only that a time attribute is a string.

cases.name: year_of_a_date_the_database_would_read_and_the_app_would_not
cases.why: u1's left_on is 2024-06-01. u2's is '20240105', whose first four characters are '2024' -- so cutting the digits out without first checking the ISO spelling would call it 2024, while the client, whose date regexp wants the dashes, calls it absent. u3 has no left_on.

cases.name: date_equality
cases.why: Only u1 was hired on 2024-03-05.
